new-and-longtime-ray-peat-followers-pers.author: GatsbyYak
new-and-longtime-ray-peat-followers-pers.core: Posted in last 7 days New & Longtime Ray Peat Followers - Personal Stories What has Ray Peat’s work done for you? Journalist looking to hear your story Hi everyone, I’m a journalist working on a long-form magazine piece about Dr. Ray Peat and I’m looking for people who’d be willing to talk to me about their experiences. I’m trying to tell the story of who he was, what happened to his ideas when they spread in recent years, and above all what it’s actually like for people who use his theories in their own lives. Just to be clear: I don’t want to write a seed-oils-are-actually-really-good-for-you-trust-the-scientists-takedown. I came across Peat’s work myself about five years ago, incorporated many of his ideas into my life, and a lot of them have worked really well for me. So I’m trying to tell the story honestly, from the perspective of the people in it. That’s why I’d love to hear from you. Any kind of experience is welcome: If you’re just getting started (<-- I'd be especially interested in this one) If Peat’s ideas changed your life If it’s been mixed, it didn’t work for you, or you’ve moved on If you’ve been around since the Ray Peat Forum days, or you corresponded with Ray himself If you see something about this community that outsiders usually get wrong If you’re open to it, feel free to send me a DM. I’m also willing to talk off the record if you’re more comfortable with that. Nothing gets published without your agreement, and you can decide whether to be named or stay anonymous. If you have questions, I’m happy to share more about myself and my work in DMs!

immigration-and-asylum-lawyers-migration.core: Posted in last 7 days Immigration & Asylum Lawyers - Migration Asylum & Human Rights Podcast We’ve finally launched THRE Podcast. In 2026, with feeds dominated by short videos and fast takes, it may not seem like the obvious choice. But that is also why we felt a longer format was needed. Human rights and migration rarely fit into a headline or a Reel. They need time: for people to speak openly, for difficult questions to be asked, and for important details not to disappear. For the first episode, Ryan Cappa joined me from Boston for a conversation about what America’s immigration crackdown looks like from inside the country — and how different that reality can be from the view abroad. Getting here took time. The first episode is not perfect. But it is lively, honest, and something our team is proud to have started. We want to make something interesting and useful — and we want to make it with you. If you are an immigration or asylum lawyer in the UK, the US or elsewhere and would like to join a future conversation, please message me. And if someone comes to mind, tag them below. THRE will not be limited to one country or one format. We want to speak with lawyers and experts from different places about migration, asylum, protests and other issues affecting human rights — through both longer conversations and shorter videos. The first episode is in the comments. #HumanRights #ImmigrationLaw #THREPodcast

dayz-community-server-owners-and-admins-.headline: DayZ Community Server Owners & Admins - Update 1.30 Impact
dayz-community-server-owners-and-admins-.author: Boydy73
dayz-community-server-owners-and-admins-.core: Posted in last 7 days DayZ Community Server Owners & Admins - Update 1.30 Impact DayZ Community Server Owners/Admins – How did your servers handle Update 1.30? G'day folks. We're having the Community Manager Marks from the DayZ Dev team at Bohemia Interactive back on the live streamed podcast this Saturday/Sunday to discuss Badlands, Update 1.30 and the community's feedback. I've been reaching out to a number of established community server owners to get their thoughts on how the update went, and I've had some pretty interesting responses so far. One thing I'm particularly interested in is whether the larger, more established communities were better equipped to prepare for and manage the update, or whether everyone copped much the same headaches regardless of their size and resources. Some of the feedback suggests that having experienced developers and technical admins makes a considerable difference, particularly when it comes to identifying problems and getting things working again. But I've also heard from larger communities where one person is effectively responsible for everything technical. So, if you own, develop or help administer a DayZ community server, I'd really like to hear from you. A few things I'm interested in: Preparation: Did you run an Experimental server beforehand? Did it actually help identify and resolve problems before Stable? Resources: How big is your technical team? Do you develop your own mods or rely primarily on third-party developers? Launch: How did 1.30 go for you? Any significant downtime, broken mods, server issues or unexpected problems? Recovery: How long did it take to get everything running properly again? Are you still dealing with outstanding issues? Lessons: What would you do differently next time? More importantly, what could BI realistically do to make these updates easier for community server operators? I'm also interested in hearing whether earlier access to technical documentation, server files or DLC configuration files would have made a meaningful difference to your preparations. This isn't about having a crack at Bohemia. There's always room to criticise, but there's also been some genuinely good work in recent updates, particularly around performance. I'm interested in understanding what actually happened, what worked, what didn't, and whether there are practical improvements that could benefit everyone. Community servers are a massive part of what keeps DayZ going, and I reckon the people putting in the hours to run them deserve to have their experiences heard. I'll be raising some of these issues with Marks on Sunday, so if you've got something constructive to contribute, please share it below. Doesn't matter whether you're running a massive network or a little 20-slot server with a handful of mates. In fact, hearing from both ends of the spectrum is exactly what I'm after. Happy to credit you and your community if we use your feedback on the show, or keep you anonymous if you'd prefer. 🎙️ 87.8 Survivor FM — DayZ Podcast with Marks (Bohemia Interactive) Sunday 25 October 2026 — International Start Times 🇦🇺 Brisbane — Sun 6:00 AM 🇦🇺 Sydney / Melbourne — Sun 7:00 AM 🇦🇺 Perth — Sun 4:00 AM 🇳🇿 Auckland — Sun 9:00 AM 🇯🇵 Tokyo — Sun 5:00 AM 🇵🇭 Manila — Sun 4:00 AM 🇨🇿 Prague — Sat 10:00 PM 🇩🇪 Berlin / 🇫🇷 Paris — Sat 10:00 PM 🇬🇧 London — Sat 9:00 PM 🇿🇦 Johannesburg — Sat 10:00 PM 🇧🇷 São Paulo / Rio — Sat 5:00 PM 🇺🇸 New York / 🇨🇦 Toronto — Sat 4:00 PM 🇺🇸 Chicago — Sat 3:00 PM 🇺🇸 Los Angeles / 🇨🇦 Vancouver — Sat 1:00 PM Cheers, Boydy73 87.8 Survivor FM

women-6069-in-uk-approaching-state-pensi.author: Elizabeth Anderson
women-6069-in-uk-approaching-state-pensi.core: Posted in last 7 days Women 60-69 in UK - Approaching State Pension Age With No Pension Sandra, 65, is approaching the state pension age – a time when most people are either winding down from work or have retired already. The problem is that Sandra, from Warwickshire, has no pension savings. Over the years she's had good jobs and even ran her own business at one stage.But a series of life events and decisions mean she's not managed to save anything towards retirement. Sandra isn't alone. One in six people are approaching their late 60s without a private pension and low household savings of less than £25,000, according to the UCL Centre for Longitudinal Studies. But Sandra has such a positive attitude. It was great interviewing her for the Daily Mail (link in comments). She says: "Even if I wanted to retire I couldn't. And I’m not alone as I’ve spoken to many other women who are in the same position. But I'm not frightened. Age is just a number." Thanks to Sandra and also to Marianna Hunt at Fidelity and Gary Smith at Evelyn for their expert commentary. If you have a money story to share, please let me know. Daily Mail

ireland-and-uk-broadcasters-and-journali.headline: Ireland & UK Broadcasters & Journalists - BBC & RTÉ Cuts Impact
ireland-and-uk-broadcasters-and-journali.author: Linda Coogan Byrne
ireland-and-uk-broadcasters-and-journali.core: Posted in last 7 days Ireland & UK Broadcasters & Journalists - BBC & RTÉ Cuts Impact I’ve spent more than 20 years working with broadcasters across Ireland and the UK. I've watched a single radio play change an artist's career. I've sat in studios with some of the finest broadcasters these islands have produced. And I've watched the industry change beyond recognition over the last decade, especially the last couple of years. And now, the BBC is cutting hundreds of jobs and closing broadcast services. RTÉ was promised €260 million for 2027 and has been allocated €240 million. Nobody has yet explained exactly what the Irish public stands to lose if that shortfall remains. Meanwhile, the BBC has just launched its 24-hour news channel on YouTube, and RTÉ is celebrating growing digital audiences. So if people are still watching and listening, why are we cutting back the very people who make the programmes? And who benefits when public broadcasters have fewer journalists asking difficult questions, fewer producers championing new artists and fewer resources to cover communities outside the major cities? There's a difference between holding the BBC and RTÉ accountable for their failures and allowing those failures to become the justification for stripping them of everything worth protecting. I've written about the money, the scandals, the political decisions and the people whose livelihoods are caught in the middle. I've also shared a few memories of Terry Wogan, Pat Kenny and Aidan Butler, and the days when radio could make a career almost overnight. Are the BBC and RTÉ being reformed, or are we watching public broadcasting being hollowed out in front of us? I'd especially like to hear from broadcasters, journalists, producers, freelancers, musicians and anyone who has worked inside these institutions. What are you seeing that the rest of us aren't?
